8. X falling on April 22, was not chosen by accident. Organizers specifically selected that date because it fell neatly between spring break and final exams for college students, who were the primary target for the "teach-in" movement. The organizers hoped that if the date landed during a lull in the academic calendar, participation would be at its peak—and they were right. 9. For decades, element X was the "missing piece" in the periodic table. Chemists in the 1920s claimed to have found it several times, but these claims were later debunked. X wasn't discovered by someone looking for a new element in a mineral; it was found in trash. In 1937, Emilio Segrè and Carlo Perrier in Italy received a piece of discarded, radioactive molybdenum foil from the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California. The foil had been used in a cyclotron (a particle accelerator) and was considered "waste." By chemically analyzing this "trash," Segrè and Perrier managed to isolate the decay product that turned out to be element X. It was named ‘X' from the Greek word meaning "artificial.” Id X.
